differences: The front silhouette is substantially closer, but the lens has become an opaque milky blue panel that hides the eyes, nose, and warm face colors. It now reads as a visor rather than the reference's clear diving mask.

The side view reveals a long flat lower-muzzle shelf and a fairly vertical forehead/eye plane. The reference has a compact rounded muzzle and more continuous cheek-to-cranium curvature; increasing projection alone has not fully solved the facial shape.
The expression remains a fixed wide-eyed stare with a thin drawn smile. The reference eyes have softer upper contours and the cheek/mouth volumes create the smile rather than relying on a long line.
Fur clumps still read as isolated triangular bumps on the body surface. They are especially conspicuous in the side swim frames and do not form the reference's soft directional silhouette.

Swim frames 0–7 show alternate fin movement and small head bobbing, but the torso stays an almost unchanged straight capsule. Visible kick motion is concentrated near the lower legs/fin roots; a traveling chest-to-hip wave is not established.

Dive frames 1–3 turn the head and bend the front of the chest downward while most of the abdomen, pelvis, and tail remain nearly horizontal. Frames 4–5 recover early, so the action reads more as a nod at the neck than a full-body aquatic dive.

Bank frames 1–3 change head direction clearly, but the torso curve, hip follow, and tail settling remain weak. The moving silhouette still feels front-driven and segmented rather than like one animal carving through the water.

These eight-frame sequences establish pose progression and expose deformation distribution, but they do not establish real-time cadence, interpolation smoothness, or animation blending. The revised beaver and actual gameplay presentation were not supplied for this round.
suggestions: P1: make the lens nearly clear with only a faint cool tint and localized highlights. Preserve the black eye/nose contrast and warm facial color through it; avoid a uniform gray-blue sheet over the entire expression.

P1: round the muzzle in cross-section, shorten its flat lower shelf, and blend its sides upward into the cheeks. Tuck the underside toward the neck so the profile reads as a small soft muzzle rather than a projecting jaw slab.
P1: add a restrained upper eyelid/eye contour and shorten the mouth line; use cheek curvature to carry a relaxed cheerful expression.

P1 motion: distribute the dive curve through chest, middle spine, lower spine, and pelvis in sequence. At its peak the entire body centerline should form a clean arc, with hips and tail visibly following after the head; delay the return until the posterior body has participated.

P1 motion: make the bank a curved body action. After head anticipation, move the chest and midsection into a shallow C-curve, let the pelvis align later, and leave the tail tip trailing briefly after the chest starts to recover.

P2 motion: drive a modest forward-swim wave through the torso and hips, with a stronger hip-led kick followed by softer ankle/fin flex and a brief glide. Keep the amplitude restrained; the goal is visible phase progression, not constant wiggling.

P2: replace surface nubs with a few shallow overlapping leaf-like fur clumps emerging from broad blended roots near silhouette edges. Omit individual clumps that remain visibly wart-like at this camera distance.
After these changes, supply a brief real-time loop and the corresponding fixed-camera frames for swim, dive, and bank; retain the current front/side camera setup for a consistent comparison.
reasoning: Head scale and body continuity have improved, but face readability, muzzle anatomy, and full-body motion remain below the reference target. The sequences now verify that motion exists, yet show that most expressive deformation is still concentrated at the head and front chest.
